attractions.name: Tatsu

scary.notes: Flying coasters provoke a fear of falling more than a fear of loops: the pretzel loop flips you onto your back and pulls you through the world's largest loop of its type, and the restraint is a full harness you hang in. The fear is front-loaded — the flight sections are calm enough to enjoy the view.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into a prone-position flying seat with overhead harness. Loading takes longer than standard coasters because of the rotation from boarding to flight position. Review the official accessibility page and linked guide for current physical, transfer and restraint criteria; staff determine eligibility.

attractions.summary: The terrain-hugging flying coaster in Rapids Camp Crossing, with a pretzel loop and views over the hillside.
description: Tatsu is a B&M flying coaster officially located in Rapids Camp Crossing. Its flying position, hillside layout and pretzel loop use the mountain’s terrain as part of the experience.

Its signature is the 124-foot pretzel loop, the largest on a flying coaster when it opened: you crest a rise lying flat, the track folds you over backwards, and you pull through the loop lying on your back looking straight up at what you just fell out of. It is the single most forceful moment at this park.
Tatsu carries a 54-inch minimum. Prioritize it if it suits your party, then plan Ninja as a separate Samurai Summit stop.
experience: Boarding is standard seats, and then the floor drops and the seats rotate you forward to face the ground before the train even leaves the station. The lift hill gives you the valley in prone position — genuinely beautiful, and the calmest thirty seconds of the ride.

The drop off the summit is terrain-hugging: the track follows the hillside down, banking around the trees at speed. Then the pretzel loop — the fold-over moment every rider remembers — and a zero-g roll and inline twists on the way back toward the station.

It ends too fast for a ride this good, which is the strongest argument for re-riding. The second lap is better than the first because you know where to look: the valley on the lift, the ground rush after the loop.
tips: Consider Tatsu early if it is a party priority and operating; check the current queue before committing to the route.
Look ahead, not down, through the flight sections; the track-line perspective is the whole point of flying coasters.
The restraint clamps your calves and shoulders — glasses wearers should use a strap.
Use the official park map to plan the separate Tatsu stop in Rapids Camp Crossing and Ninja stop in Samurai Summit.
attractions.bestTime: An early stop can fit a priority plan; current queues and operations decide the timing.
attractions.typicalWait: No current numerical wait forecast verified. Check the official app and attraction queue on your visit date.

faqs.q: Can I compare Tatsu and X2 on a current visit?
faqs.a: Tatsu remains a current riding option, subject to daily operations and restrictions. X2 is permanently retired; its preserved page is historical, so it cannot be part of a current ride comparison itinerary.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for Tatsu?
faqs.a: 54 inches, the standard minimum for the park's biggest B&M coasters. There is no 48-inch tier on this one.

faqs.q: Does the pretzel loop make people sick?
faqs.a: It is the highest-force moment at the park, and motion-sensitive riders do struggle with it. The flight sections before and after are gentle by comparison. If you are prone to motion sickness, ride it before lunch, not after.

attractions.name: Twisted Colossus

scary.notes: A wooden coaster in appearance and an aggressive steel hybrid in behaviour. The first drop is steep and the inversions surprise riders expecting a classic woodie. Nothing here is frightening beyond the physical — it is airtime and laterals, not fear.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into standard coaster trains with lap-bar restraints. The lap-bar-only restraint makes this one of the more accommodative big coasters for larger riders. Review the official accessibility page and linked guide for current physical, transfer and restraint criteria; staff determine eligibility.

attractions.summary: The 1978 racing wooden twins rebuilt in steel — now a single hybrid that races its own second train and high-fives its own track twice.
description: Colossus was Magic Mountain's racing wooden coaster from 1978, famous from film and famous for its white structure. In 2015 Rocky Mountain Construction rebuilt it as Twisted Colossus: the wooden structure remains, the track became the inversions-capable Ibox steel, and the two original tracks became one continuous circuit ridden by two trains that can race.

The result is the park's most re-ridable big coaster. Two inversions — including the vaunted Top Gun stall where the track banks and hangs — plus airtime hills that modern wood-hybrid riders cross the country for. When both trains dispatch in sequence, they duel side by side up the lift and through the first half, and the race is the show.

The 48-inch minimum makes it the family threshold ride: the coaster a twelve-year-old graduates onto before they are tall enough for Tatsu. For mixed-height parties it is the park's most valuable coaster.
experience: The first drop is a double-down rebuilt steeper than wood allowed, and the pace never settles afterward. The sequence runs a zero-g roll, the high-five bank where two trains pass within arm's reach of each other's track, and the long stall where you hang sideways staring at the structure.

If the race is on — two trains, staggered dispatch — the second lap energy changes completely: riders on both trains scream at each other across the parallel lifts, and the operators lean into it. Ask at the station whether the duel dispatch is running; on light days they will sometimes hold a train to make it happen.

The back half is a terrain-hugging return through the old Colossus footprint, all laterals and pops of airtime. It is the rare big coaster that gets better the more tired you are, because the restraints are lap bars and your body has nothing to fight.
tips: Ask the station crew if the racing dispatch is running — the high-five element only happens when both trains duel.
Ride the back car for airtime, the front for the race view; there is no wrong row on this one.
The 48-inch minimum plus lap-bar restraints make this the best first big coaster at the park.
Consider an afternoon stop if its current queue and operation fit the plan; it is not a guaranteed quiet window.
attractions.bestTime: Check the current queue in Screampunk District; afternoon waits vary by day.
attractions.typicalWait: No current numerical wait forecast verified. Check the official app and attraction queue on your visit date.

faqs.q: Is Twisted Colossus a wooden coaster?
faqs.a: It is a hybrid: the original 1978 wooden structure supports new steel Ibox track, which is what lets it invert. It looks like a woodie and rides like a modern steel coaster, which is exactly the appeal.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement?
faqs.a: 48 inches — the threshold tier at this park, and lower than the 54-inch big B&Ms. It is the natural first big coaster for kids who have just crossed 48.

faqs.q: What is the 'high five' element?
faqs.a: Two points on the dueling tracks bank toward each other so the racing trains pass close enough that riders could theoretically slap hands. It only happens when both trains are dispatched in race sequence.

attractions.name: Goliath

scary.notes: The large drop, tunnel and sustained helix create speed, darkness and force sensations. These are separate from the 48-inch minimum; check the physical restrictions and your own tolerance.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into traditional coaster trains. The final brake run and unload are ground level. Review the official accessibility page and linked guide for current physical, transfer and restraint criteria; staff determine eligibility.

attractions.summary: The Giovanola hypercoaster with a major first drop, an underground tunnel and a sustained helix.
description: Goliath opened in 2000 and combines a large drop, high speed, a tunnel and an extended helix. The helix’s sustained forces are part of the experience; this guide does not predict a rider’s medical response.

It carries a 48-inch minimum despite being one of the biggest drops at the park, which is the standing surprise of Magic Mountain's height ladder. The restraint is a lap bar, the seats are roomy, and the ride is speed-and-airtime rather than inversions.

The mid-course underground tunnel is the moment non-enthusiasts remember: full darkness at full speed, then daylight and the helix. Goliath does not have Tatsu's flying position — it is simply enormous, and enormously re-ridable.
experience: The lift gives you the whole back corner of the park, then the drop. Sixty-one degrees from 255 feet is a commitment the stomach registers before the brain does. The first hill's airtime float leads straight into the tunnel — dark, loud, disorienting for exactly the right number of seconds.
The second half includes a sustained helix. Assess that element with the ride’s posted health and physical restrictions rather than relying on a promise about how it will feel.
The layout has no inversions, so it may appeal to riders avoiding loops. Its large drop, speed and sustained helix remain significant demands; a height minimum does not measure intensity tolerance.
tips: Choose a row for the view and ride experience without assuming a predictable physical or medical response.
If tunnels in darkness are a no for a young rider, this is not the intro coaster — the tunnel is fast and total.
Check the current queue when you reach Goliath Plaza; do not assume an afternoon wait.
Follow the ride’s posted health restrictions and attraction staff’s directions; hydration does not establish fitness to ride.
attractions.bestTime: Use the current Goliath Plaza queue and party priorities; no particular hour is guaranteed.
attractions.typicalWait: No current numerical wait forecast verified. Check the official app and attraction queue on your visit date.

faqs.q: Does Goliath really make people black out?
faqs.a: The helix pulls sustained positive g-force that causes brief grey-outs for some riders, especially in the front row. It is a known, discussed, and for many riders sought-after feature of the ride. It passes within seconds and is not a medical event for healthy riders, but anyone with cardiovascular concerns should skip it.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement?
faqs.a: 48 inches — surprisingly low for a 255-foot drop, and one of the reasons this park is so good for the 48-to-54 crowd.

faqs.q: Is Goliath scary for kids at 48 inches?
faqs.a: The drop is the scariest single moment, and the tunnel darkness surprises first-timers. Kids who handle Twisted Colossus usually handle Goliath; kids who found Colossus at the edge should wait a season.

attractions.heightNote: 54-inch minimum. Official source: https://www.sixflags.com/magicmountain/attractions/full-throttle. attractions.summary: The Six Flags Plaza launch coaster: 70 mph, a 160-foot loop and a backwards launch from its tunnel.
description: Full Throttle is a Premier launch coaster in Six Flags Plaza. Six Flags lists a launch speed of 70 mph, a 160-foot loop and a 54-inch minimum. After stopping inside a tunnel, the train launches backwards before returning through the tunnel and over the outside of the loop.
The launches, backwards movement and loop define the ride. Check the park’s official attraction page for current operating information and all restrictions.
At 54 inches it sits in the big-kid tier. For coaster-counting visitors it is a marquee credit; for families it is the one that sits at the top of the 'maybe next year' list.
experience: From a complete stop, the launch reaches 70 mph into the 160-foot loop. The speed and change in orientation are the defining sensations.
The train stops in the tunnel and launches backwards. It then returns through the tunnel and travels around the outside of the loop, with hangtime near the top.
Consider Full Throttle when passing through Six Flags Plaza, subject to current operations and queues. An opening-time or late-day stop does not guarantee a short wait.
tips: Check the current queue and closing time before choosing a late-day Full Throttle stop.
The backwards launch is the surprise; brace your neck against the headrest before the second launch.
Use designated spectator areas in Six Flags Plaza and follow posted boundaries.

faqs.q: Is Full Throttle scary?
faqs.a: The official ride description lists a 70-mph launch, a 160-foot loop and a backwards launch out of the tunnel. Those elements can challenge riders uneasy with speed, inversion or backwards movement.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for Full Throttle?
faqs.a: 54 inches. West Coast Racers also requires 54 inches. faqs.q: Does Full Throttle go backwards?

faqs.q: How fast is Full Throttle?

attractions.summary: Side-by-side racing launches in The Underground, with four inversions: three zero-G rolls and one zero-G stall.
description: West Coast Racers is a Premier racing launch coaster in The Underground. Six Flags lists a 54-inch minimum and four inversions: three zero-G rolls and one zero-G stall. The side-by-side racing format combines launches, crossings and changes in orientation.

The racing format gives it show value that single-track coasters lack: the two tracks cross and parallel each other constantly, and the outcome is different every cycle depending on dispatch timing. The pit-station theming — cars pulling in for tire changes mid-race — is the most complete theming at this park since the 1990s.
Choose it for riders comfortable with launches and inversions. Its racing format does not make it an inversion-free alternative or establish that a motion-sensitive rider will tolerate it.
experience: Two tracks, two trains, and a race that is genuinely undecided every cycle. The four launches between the sides mean the lead swaps, and the crossings come close enough that the other train fills your peripheral vision mid-twist.
The four inversions include three zero-G rolls and one zero-G stall. These changes in orientation are part of the experience, so riders avoiding inversions should choose a different attraction.

The pit-station theming — cars pulling in mid-race for tire changes — gives the racing format a distinct identity. Allow for the full launch-and-inversion experience when deciding whether it suits your party.
tips: Both tracks ride differently — ask which is the red/blue side and do both if the queue allows.
The racing outcome depends on dispatch timing; midday dispatches are likelier to be true side-by-side.
Plan a separate stop in The Underground; West Coast Racers is not in Cyclone Bay.

faqs.q: Is West Coast Racers scary?

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for West Coast Racers?

faqs.q: Do the two West Coast Racers tracks really race?
faqs.a: Yes, when dispatch timing cooperates. The two trains genuinely race through crossings and helixes and the outcome differs every cycle — that is the show. Pick the side dispatching second if you want to chase rather than be chased.

attractions.name: Viper

scary.notes: Seven inversions including a batwing and double corkscrew, on 1990 Arrow track — meaning the transitions are abrupt where modern coasters are sculpted. Head-bang risk is real for riders who do not pin their heads back.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into Arrow-style trains with over-the-shoulder restraints. Review the official accessibility page and linked guide for current physical, transfer and restraint criteria; staff determine eligibility.

attractions.summary: The 1990 Arrow multilooper with seven inversions and the interlocking corkscrews every visitor photographs from the parking lot.
description: Viper is the classic that refuses to leave: a 144-foot first drop into a vertical loop, a batwing, and the interlocking corkscrew finale that has been the park's silhouette since 1990. It was among the tallest looping coasters in the world on opening and remains the purest old-school looper at the park.

Riding Viper is a technique exercise. Arrow transitions snap between elements, and the over-shoulder harness punishes loose heads — keep pinned to the headrest and the ride is a blast; fight it and you will finish with a headache. Enthusiasts who grew up on Arrow track regard Viper as a rite; first-timers should treat it as one too.
The ridge setting can make Viper an appealing late-day stop if it is operating and suitable for your party. That is a planning suggestion, not a prediction of the shortest queue.
experience: Follow attraction staff’s instructions for the restraint, head position and riding posture. The older track’s transitions may feel abrupt; no posture technique guarantees comfort or avoids a headache.

The sequence is the 1990s in order: a 144-foot drop into a vertical loop, a batwing that folds the train through itself, and the interlocking corkscrew finale that has been the park’s silhouette since 1990. It was among the tallest looping coasters in the world when it opened, and the scale still reads from the queue.
Consider a late-day Viper stop if the operating hours, current queue and your return plan fit. A sunset visit does not guarantee a shorter wait.
tips: Use the current queue and operating hours to decide whether a late-day stop fits.
Save it for the golden hour; the ridge view plus short queue is the best late-day pairing.
Skip it if anyone in the party is prone to headaches or neck issues; nothing at the park punishes tension like Viper.

faqs.a: The older track’s transitions may feel abrupt. Follow the attraction staff’s restraint and posture instructions; comfort varies by rider and no technique guarantees a comfortable ride.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for Viper?
faqs.a: 54 inches. It shares the big-kid tier with Tatsu, Full Throttle, Batman and Riddler’s Revenge.

faqs.q: How many inversions does Viper have?

attractions.name: Batman: The Ride

scary.notes: Compact invert, relentless pacing, five inversions in a small footprint. The forces are higher than the ride's size suggests — the vertical loop and zero-g roll come fast and the finale helix pulls hard. Riders who find big drops scary handle Batman; riders who hate quick direction changes do not.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into suspended invert trains with floor-drop loading. Review the official accessibility page and linked guide for current physical, transfer and restraint criteria; staff determine eligibility.

attractions.summary: The West Coast Batman invert — the 1994 B&M suspended coaster that still out-punches rides twice its footprint.
description: Magic Mountain's Batman is the West Coast sibling of the 1992 Great America original, a first-generation B&M invert packing a vertical loop, zero-g roll, corkscrews and tight helixes into one of the smallest big-coaster footprints anywhere. Thirty years on, it remains the pacing benchmark other compact loopers are measured against.

Because the layout is short and the trains never stop fighting, Batman is the purest forty-five seconds of intensity at the park. The suspended seats swing through the elements; the front row gets the cleanest inversion sensations, the back row gets whipped hardest.
Its listed minimum is 54 inches. Batman: The Ride is officially in DC UNIVERSE; The Riddler’s Revenge belongs to METROPOLIS, and height alone does not establish permission to ride.
experience: Your feet hang and the train never stops fighting. A vertical loop, a zero-g roll, corkscrews and hard helixes arrive with no filler between them — the layout is too short for any — which makes this the purest sustained forty-five seconds of intensity at the park.

Row choice is a real decision. The front row gets the cleanest inversion sensations and the view of the track snapping away underneath you; the back row gets whipped hardest through the same elements. The ride is short enough to do both when the queue allows.
Batman remains a compact inversion coaster in DC UNIVERSE. The Riddler’s Revenge is a separate stand-up coaster in METROPOLIS rather than another ride assigned to this land.
tips: Front row for the flight sensation; back row for force.
The queue is shaded and themed — one of the few at this park where the wait itself is tolerable at midday.
Plan Batman in DC UNIVERSE and Riddler’s Revenge in METROPOLIS as separate land stops.

faqs.q: Is Batman: The Ride scary?
faqs.a: The forces are higher than the ride’s size suggests — the vertical loop and zero-g roll come fast and the finale helix pulls hard. Riders who find big drops scary handle Batman fine; riders who hate quick direction changes do not.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for Batman: The Ride?
faqs.a: 54 inches is the listed minimum. Batman is officially in DC UNIVERSE; all other posted restrictions and the attraction staff’s decision still apply.

faqs.q: Which row is best on Batman: The Ride?
faqs.a: The front for the cleanest inversion sensations and the view of the track snapping away underneath you; the back to be whipped hardest through the same elements. The layout is short enough that both are worth a lap when the queue allows.

attractions.name: The Riddler's Revenge

scary.notes: Standing up through six inversions is a strange, exposed feeling — the restraint is a bicycle-style seat and a harness, and every loop is felt differently than seated. The fear is novelty rather than menace; the forces are B&M-smooth.

accessibility.notes: Transfer into stand-up trains; the boarding cycle includes adjusting the bicycle seat height, which takes longer than standard loading. Review the official accessibility page and linked guide for current physical, transfer and restraint criteria; staff determine eligibility.

attractions.summary: The world's tallest and fastest stand-up coaster — six inversions taken standing up, a category of ride that barely still exists.
description: The Riddler's Revenge is a 156-foot B&M stand-up coaster and the last of its size anywhere: stand-up coasters stopped being built, and the survivors are aging monuments. Riding it means standing against a bicycle seat through a vertical loop, two dive loops, an inclined loop and corkscrews — inversions feel categorically different on your feet.

The technique matters: stand straight with the seat at the right height, and the ride is smooth; slouch or lean, and the restraints correct you at speed. First-timers should watch the load cycle once to see the posture.
Six Flags officially places The Riddler’s Revenge in METROPOLIS. Batman: The Ride is a separate stop in DC UNIVERSE, so use the current park map when planning both.
experience: You stand the whole ride: a bicycle-style seat takes your weight, a harness clamps your torso, and the train leaves with you vertical. The first inversion is the adjustment lap — standing through a loop is a categorically different sensation, felt through your legs and spine instead of your shoulders.

Have attraction staff explain the stand-up restraint setting and correct riding posture. Copying another rider’s appearance is not an eligibility or safety assessment, and posture does not guarantee comfort.

This is the last stand-up coaster of its size anywhere. Stand-ups stopped being built, and the survivors are working artifacts — as much museum as ride. Ride it for what it is, because nothing new will ever be it.
tips: Get the seat height right at boarding — adjusting mid-ride is impossible and the wrong height hurts.
Stand tall through the loops; leaning into the harness is how riders end up sore.
Check the current Riddler’s Revenge queue in METROPOLIS rather than assuming a longer wait than Batman in DC UNIVERSE.

faqs.q: Is The Riddler’s Revenge painful?
faqs.a: Comfort varies in the stand-up restraint. Follow staff’s fitting and posture instructions and the posted physical requirements rather than assuming a particular posture prevents pain.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for The Riddler’s Revenge?
faqs.a: 54 inches. The restraint is a bicycle-style seat and a harness rather than a lap bar, so fit matters — attendants set the seat height per rider, and you want your legs slightly bent, not locked straight.

faqs.q: Do you really stand up the whole ride?
faqs.a: Yes — that is the entire concept. The train leaves with you vertical, and all six inversions are felt through your legs and spine instead of your shoulders. It is the last stand-up coaster of its size anywhere, which makes it a working artifact as much as a ride.

riderRestrictions: The official accessibility page says guests with any prostheses are not permitted on this attraction. Its separate supplemental-harness criteria address certain amputations; consult the Ride Information Center and attraction staff about the applicable criteria. Source: https://www.sixflags.com/magicmountain/accessibility

scary.notes: A suspended swinging coaster through real trees — the motion is gliding, not violent. The summit location adds height exposure in a couple of spots. This is the mountain's best coaster for the 42-to-48 crowd and nervous adults building tolerance.

attractions.summary: The 1988 suspended coaster that swings through the summit's trees — the mountain's family coaster and its most beautiful ride.
description: Ninja is an Arrow suspended coaster, one of the last running: trains hang from the track and swing outward on every curve, and the layout threads through actual trees on the mountainside below the summit. Opened in 1988, it is the gentlest way to see why this park's terrain matters.

The swings are the ride — no inversions, no launches, just pendulum turns through pine canopy with the valley appearing between branches. At 42 inches it is the summit's entry coaster and the single best ride at the park for the height bracket between Ninja's minimum and the 48-inch big tier.
For coaster historians it is a working museum piece; for eight-year-olds it is the best ride on the mountain. Both are correct.
experience: The trains hang from the rail and swing outward on every curve, so the whole ride is a pendulum conversation between the track and gravity. No inversions, no launches — the lift takes you up through the trees and the layout spends that elevation gliding.

It threads actual pines on the mountainside below the summit, and the valley appears between branches on the outer swings. Of everything at this park, Ninja is the gentlest demonstration of why a mountain is better than flatland to build on.
Ninja is a surviving Arrow suspended coaster with a 42-inch minimum and separate physical requirements. Its historical interest and gentler profile do not predict a short queue or permission to ride.
tips: The queue is one of the shadiest at the park — a good midday escape.
Plan Ninja in Samurai Summit and Tatsu in Rapids Camp Crossing using the current park map.
Sit mid-train: the swing amplitude is pleasant there and aggressive at the ends.

faqs.q: Is Ninja scary?
faqs.a: No. The motion is gliding, not violent — trains hang from the track and swing outward on every curve through real trees. A couple of spots add height exposure from the summit location, but this is the mountain’s best coaster for nervous riders building tolerance.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for Ninja?
faqs.a: 42 inches. It is the lowest minimum among the current coasters this guide tracks at Magic Mountain. Gold Rusher requires 48 inches and is not an alternative for a rider below 42 inches.

faqs.q: Does Ninja go upside down?
faqs.a: No inversions and no launches. The suspended trains swing outward on the curves, which delivers the sensation without flipping anyone — the interest is motion and terrain, not elements.

riderRestrictions: Maintain an upright seated position with the head against the headrest and keep arms, hands, legs and feet inside the vehicle.
Step up and down into the vehicle; wheelchair users must transfer to the ride vehicle.

The official guide requires at least one functioning arm and one functioning leg. A full-body harness may permit riding when the extremity requirements are not met, if the harness manufacturer’s requirements are satisfied. Ask attraction staff to assess the applicable criteria.

scary.notes: A 1971 mine train: small dips, mild speed, one short tunnel. The first roller coaster for many Southern California children across three generations.

attractions.summary: The 1971 mine train that opened with the park — the mountain's first coaster and still its gentlest.
description: Gold Rusher predates everything else at Magic Mountain: it opened with the park on day one in May 1971, and its lift, tunnel and dip course have introduced children to roller coasters for over fifty years. It is small, slow and completely unbothered by any of the records its neighbors chase.

As an introduction to coasters it offers a real lift hill, a small drop and a dark tunnel. The official minimum is 48 inches, regardless of age, and the official location is METROPOLIS. The historical spelling Goldrusher remains useful when searching older guides.
experience: A chain lift, small drops and a short tunnel introduce the mine-train ride style. Plan for a rider who meets the 48-inch minimum and the attraction’s other requirements; age alone is no guide to eligibility.

It opened with the park on day one in May 1971, which makes it the oldest ride on the mountain and the only one that predates every record its neighbors chase. The dips are mild, the speed is polite, and it is completely unbothered by all of it.

Ride it for one of two reasons: you have a first-timer with you, or you care that this is the mine train that introduced three generations of Southern California children to coasters. There is no third reason, and neither of those needs one.
tips: Gold Rusher can be a gentler warm-up for suitable riders; check its current queue rather than assuming a walk-on.
The tunnel adds a brief dark section; prepare first-time riders who are uneasy in darkness.
Use it as a gentler warm-up for eligible riders at 48 inches or taller; it is not an under-48-inch option.
attractions.bestTime: Choose the stop using the current METROPOLIS queue and operations.
attractions.typicalWait: No current numerical wait forecast verified. Check the official app and attraction queue on your visit date.

faqs.q: Is Gold Rusher scary?
faqs.a: No. Small dips, mild speed and one short tunnel — the brake run arrives before anyone can get scared. It has been the first roller coaster for three generations of Southern California children, which is the design brief working as intended.

faqs.q: What is the height requirement for Gold Rusher?
faqs.a: 48 inches, according to Six Flags’ official attraction page. It is in METROPOLIS. All other ride restrictions still apply, and attraction staff make the final eligibility determination.

faqs.q: Why is Gold Rusher worth riding?
faqs.a: History, mostly. It opened with the park on day one in May 1971 and predates every record its neighbors chase. Ride it with a first-timer, or ride it because it is the oldest thing on the mountain — there is no third reason.

riderRestrictions: Maintain an upright seated position with the back against the seatback and keep arms, hands, legs and feet inside the vehicle.
Step up and down into the vehicle; wheelchair users must transfer to the ride vehicle.

The official guide requires at least three functioning appendages: one arm and two legs, or two arms and one leg. A full-body harness may permit riding when the extremity requirements are not met, if the harness manufacturer’s requirements are satisfied. Ask attraction staff to assess the applicable criteria.
